reference.source: Respiratory Medicine and Interventional Radiology reference texts
clinicalPearls: An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and vein that bypasses the capillary bed, creating a right-to-left shunt
The majority are associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease), so screening and family assessment are important
The right-to-left shunt causes hypoxaemia, and the loss of capillary filtration allows paradoxical embolism, predisposing to stroke and brain abscess
Classic features include dyspnoea, cyanosis, digital clubbing, and, when related to HHT, epistaxis and mucocutaneous telangiectasia
Platypnoea and orthodeoxia (breathlessness and desaturation on sitting or standing) can occur with basal lesions
Contrast (bubble) echocardiography is a sensitive screening test for right-to-left shunt, with CT pulmonary angiography defining the feeding vessels
Transcatheter embolisation of feeding arteries is the mainstay of treatment and reduces the risk of neurological complications and haemorrhage
reference.pathophysiology: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation is a thin-walled abnormal vascular sac or channel connecting a feeding pulmonary artery directly to a draining pulmonary vein, bypassing the normal capillary network. This produces a right-to-left shunt that lowers arterial oxygenation and, critically, removes the capillary filter that normally traps small emboli and bacteria, so venous clots and septic material can pass directly into the systemic circulation and cause paradoxical stroke and cerebral abscess. Most lesions arise in the context of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant disorder of vascular development, and they tend to enlarge over time and during pregnancy. The fragile vessel walls can also rupture, causing haemoptysis or haemothorax.
additionalDifferentials: Intracardiac right-to-left shunt (e.g. patent foramen ovale, atrial septal defect)
Solitary pulmonary nodule of other aetiology
Other causes of hypoxaemia and clubbing
additionalInvestigations: Contrast (agitated saline bubble) echocardiography to detect and grade right-to-left shunt
CT pulmonary angiography to characterise feeding and draining vessels
Shunt fraction estimation (e.g. by the 100% oxygen method or nuclear perfusion scan)
Screening and genetic assessment for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Cerebral imaging when neurological symptoms or abscess are suspected
Assessment for anaemia and iron deficiency from associated bleeding
redFlags: Neurological symptoms suggesting paradoxical stroke or cerebral abscess
Massive haemoptysis or haemothorax from lesion rupture
Enlarging lesions, especially during pregnancy, increasing complication risk
reference.prognosis: With embolisation of the feeding arteries, oxygenation improves and the risk of serious neurological and haemorrhagic complications falls substantially; untreated lesions carry a significant risk of stroke, brain abscess, and life-threatening haemorrhage, and lifelong surveillance is needed as lesions can recur or grow.
pitfalls: Failing to consider a pulmonary AVM in unexplained hypoxaemia, clubbing, or paradoxical embolism
Not screening for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and missing familial disease
Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis advice for procedures given the risk of brain abscess
Overlooking small lesions that still permit paradoxical embolism despite minimal hypoxaemia
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
International guidelines on hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
